html:
The near destruction of the American bison on the Great Plains by commercial hunters, mostly between 1872 and 1884. Tens of millions of bison had roamed the plains; by the late 1880s only a few hundred were left in the wild.

New tanning methods made bison hides valuable for leather, especially for machine belts in factories, and the new railways could carry them east. Hunters with long range rifles shot thousands each, took the hides and left the meat to rot. The southern herd went first, in the 1870s, the northern herd in the early 1880s.

For the Lakota, Cheyenne, Comanche and other Plains peoples, the bison was food, clothing, shelter and the centre of their religion. Many army officers and officials welcomed the killing, since it forced these peoples onto reservations. Leaders like Sitting Bull surrendered as their people starved. A few private herds survived, and conservation from the 1900s brought the bison back from the edge. It had been central to Plains life since horses arrived.
